phases: What a Page Does Not Say

listenings.text: I have sat through maybe two hundred vendor pitches and I now ask the same four questions every time, in the same order, and I ask them out loud in the meeting rather than afterwards in an email. One. What exactly happens on day one if we say yes. Not the vision, the first two weeks. Two. Which of your existing clients is closest to us in size and in regulation, and can I call them. Three. What breaks first when the volume triples. Every system breaks somewhere and I would rather hear it from you than find it myself. And four. What would you need from my side that you have not asked for yet. That last one is the most useful question in the room, because it moves them from selling to planning, and you learn immediately whether they have actually done this before.

I sell to banks for a living, so let me tell you what happens on our side of the table. When a bank asks me for a reference client in the same regulatory environment, I know the deal is real and I take it to my head of delivery that evening. When a bank asks only about price in the first meeting, I quote high, because price is the only thing they have given me to compete on. And when somebody asks what breaks first at three times the volume, I will be honest with you, half of my competitors cannot answer that question at all. So the questions do not just get you information. They tell me who I am dealing with, and they change what I bring to the second meeting.

There is a pattern in failed technology procurement that shows up again and again in the reviews afterwards, and it is almost never about the technology. The decision goes wrong at the point where the buying side accepts a claim without turning it into a condition. A supplier says integration typically takes twelve weeks. Typically. Nobody asks what would make it twenty, and twenty is what it becomes. A supplier says the platform scales. Nobody asks to what, or what happens at the point where it stops. The fix is not scepticism and it is not more meetings. It is one habit, which is to turn every claim on the page into a sentence beginning with if. If the integration runs past sixteen weeks, then what. If the regulator changes the reporting rule in March, then what. A claim you cannot turn into an if is usually a claim the supplier has not tested either.

reading.rtitle: The Claim Nobody Turned Into a Condition
paras: Every failed technology purchase produces a review afterwards, and the reviews are remarkably similar. They almost never blame the technology. They blame a sentence on page two that everybody read and nobody questioned.

The sentence usually contains the word typically. Integration typically takes twelve weeks. Onboarding is typically complete within a month. The word is doing an enormous amount of work: it tells you what happens in the good case, and it says nothing at all about the bad one. Twelve becomes twenty, and the twenty was never a surprise to the vendor — it was simply never asked about.

Rania Faress, who has run procurement for two European banks, describes the fix as a single habit rather than a mindset. “I am not more suspicious than anybody else,” she says. “I just turn every claim on the page into a sentence that starts with if. If the integration runs past sixteen weeks, what happens to the fee. If the regulator changes the reporting rule in March, who absorbs the work. If the volume triples in year two, what breaks first.” She says the answers matter less than people expect. “A claim the supplier cannot turn into an if is usually a claim they have not tested either.”

The same habit reshapes how the numbers are read. A proof of concept that runs for six weeks with two clients proves that the idea works at all; it proves nothing about year three. A return on investment of eighteen months is a promise, not a measurement, and the useful question is which assumption inside it is the fragile one. And a cost-benefit analysis that has no trade-off written down anywhere is not an analysis. It is a brochure.

Faress keeps one page of her own next to every proposal she reads. On it are the four or five things the solution has to do before the conversation is even worth having — her requirements, in her words, not theirs. “The proposal is written to be agreed with,” she says. “My page is written to be checked against. If I read theirs without mine open, I will agree with it, because it is very well written and that is what it was built for.”
